title: Mirrors and Walls: Dumont and Cultural Barriers
intro: One essay from the inside, then the mainstream it pushes against. Start Assignment 3.1 here.

terms.def: A rigid, oversimplified belief about a whole group, applied to every member regardless of reality.
Anything blocking full participation, from stereotypes and discrimination to policies built for someone else.

body: Jenine Dumont's 1990 essay opens the chapter from the inside. Born in 1944 at Duck Lake to a grandnephew of Gabriel Dumont, she grew up hearing her ancestor called infamous in school while her own people called him famous. At six she looked at her newborn sister and said she looks like an Indian, not knowing she was part Indian herself; after a teacher singled out her brother's family in social studies, years of half-breed taunting followed, her brother dropped out at fourteen, and only then did her father begin the counter-lesson, hold your head up high and be proud. Even her mother called Indians les sauvages, the savages, and Dumont keeps asking which words, Indian or First Nations person, change what the story can do.

The essay asks what mainstream even means. Mainstream names the ideas, values, and behaviours a country's majority accepts, reinforced the way a shared belief, that the world is round, becomes the only belief imaginable. Before the nineteenth century, First Nations and Inuit worldviews were North America's mainstream; after Confederation in 1867, Euro-Canadian worldviews took over government, economics, and society, and have set the terms ever since.

Against that current runs assimilation, adopting mainstream values to fit in. Sometimes it is natural, like intermarriage alliances where a newcomer takes a spouse's ways, and the chapter's river image asks whether it is easier to swim with the main stream or fight upstream, especially with fences blocking the water. Immigrants often choose the current, learning English or French and lining up at citizenship ceremonies, and Nisga'a leaders even spoke of negotiating their way into Canada. But First Nations, Métis, and Inuit peoples are Canada's only minority that is not immigrant at all, and despite centuries of pressure to assimilate, most never did.

The stakes are freedom to choose: full contributing membership in Canada while remaining culturally distinct, the right to participate but stay different. Cultural barriers, the alienation Dumont describes, block that middle way, and stereotypes are their engine. A stereotype is rigid, oversimplified, often exaggerated, the feathered headdress and prairie horse pasted onto peoples who never lived that way. It works as a lens that makes the stereotyped person look odd, survives meetings with real individuals by filing them as exceptions, and harms even when positive, since calling women naturally nurturing still erases individual difference. Read the census pages with the same suspicion the chapter teaches: the 2001 Aboriginal Peoples Survey only means what its surveyed slice lets it mean.

example.title: Assignment 3.1 starts here
example.text: Assignment 3.1 asks for two media stereotypes plus a supported opinion on perpetuation and battle. Bank the headdress-and-horse stereotype from this lesson with its page reference, and find your second in the Tiger Lily, Racist History of Peter Pan, or Reel Injun videos.

check.prompt: How did schooling shape Dumont's view of her own family?
check.sample: Sample response: classroom history framed her ancestor's side as infamous, so she applied the stigma to her own newborn sister, then watched a teacher's singling-out turn classmates' taunts on her family until her brother dropped out.

title: Words That Wound: Discrimination, Columbus, Littlechild
intro: The chain from stereotype to unequal treatment, and two men who answer it.

terms.def: Acting on prejudice, overtly in open exclusion or covertly in quiet denials of opportunity.
Cree lawyer, athlete, and MP whose skungun teaching defends sharing land while reserving ceremony and sanctuary.

body: Stereotypes feed prejudice, a preconceived idea, and prejudice becomes discrimination the moment it acts: treating people unequally because one group is judged inferior. The chapter sorts the acting four ways. Overt discrimination shows itself, like refusing someone entry to a business, while covert discrimination hides, like never hiring the qualified woman who never learns why. Blatant discrimination is conscious, deliberate, and illegal, a For Rent sign barring minorities lands the landlord in court, while subtle discrimination leaves no proof, the same sign with no minorities ever chosen. Conscious or unconscious, verbal slur or non-verbal rolled eyes, sigh, and stare, the machinery is the same: unequal treatment justified by a fixed picture.

Then comes the case study in words as barriers. When countries planned to celebrate the 1992 quincentenary of Columbus's discovery of the New World, Aboriginal groups across the Americas answered nearly as one: the beginning of their domination is nothing to celebrate, and lands their ancestors had called home for centuries were never discovered. Dismissing this as just words misses the chapter's point, which Lee Curotte of Kahnawake made visible in 2003 by hanging a Columbus Invaded America banner on a Massasoit statue at Plymouth. Language used with sensitivity builds openness and trust; inclusive language keeps everyone inside the community it describes.

Willie Littlechild answers with a Cree word worth more than a chapter. Skungun means that at treaty time the parties agreed to share everything, surface rights to the land, while each reserved a small portion for ceremony and traditional pursuits. Against politicians chanting we should all be equal, which really means no unique rights at all, Littlechild sets a spiritual relationship to Mother Earth that dominant society, pricing land as real estate, cannot see. His life backs the word: first Treaty Indian from Alberta to graduate law school in 1976, athlete in more than thirty-five championships, MP for Wetaskiwin from 1988 to 1993, advocate at the UN, the International Labour Organization, and the Organization of American States, and Rapporteur helping build the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.

Law can stop the blatant, but only changed attitudes stop the subtle, which is where education enters. Teaching empathy and compassion, the imaginative step into another's perspective, prevents discrimination before it acts, and simply naming the stereotypes around us drains their power, though they hide in rarely questioned habits. The next two lessons tour the hiding places, language, film, television, art, marketing, and humour, so keep 3.1's collection open: this lesson's discrimination chain is the opinion half of that paragraph waiting for its examples.

example.title: Work the chain
example.text: Take one stereotype and run it down the chain: the fixed picture (headdress past), the prejudice (all Aboriginal people live there), the discrimination (overt hiring refusal or covert never-called-back). Then flip it with Littlechild: what does skungun require instead?

check.prompt: Contrast blatant and subtle discrimination using the chapter's For Rent example.
check.sample: Sample response: a sign barring minorities is blatant, conscious, and illegal; the same apartment that simply never goes to minority applicants is subtle and unprovable, which is why subtle discrimination is harder to fight.

title: Screens and Punchlines: Media, Humour, Identity
intro: The tools that spread stereotypes, turned around to break them.

terms.def: The Alexander First Nation comedian who twists racist jokes back on racism itself.
A fixed picture absorbed so deeply that stereotyped people apply it to themselves.

body: Language is the first tool because words are symbols carrying history. Indian is not bad in itself, but used for generations to offend and exclude, it accumulates offense. Labels work the same way: the late moviegoer becomes inconsiderate people, and if the late person belongs to a visible minority, the label spreads to the whole group, shrinking people to adjectives like lazy or heathen and stripping their humanity.

Film and television industrialized the labels. Early Hollywood westerns put made-up, makeup-wearing bad guys on screen to heighten suspense, shaping the mainstream image for generations, and some Aboriginal viewers internalized the pictures, replacing real knowledge of their own cultures. Newer bottles hold old wine: the eco-guardian stereotype flatters while still erasing individual difference, and TV news covers Aboriginal peoples heavily but mostly as problems costing money or threatening violence. Stan Isadore learned this in Spain, where theatregoers greeted him with HOW! because movies were all they knew, and even Jay Silverheels, the Six Nations actor behind Tonto, could not escape his character's frame.

The counterattack runs on the same frequencies. The Inuit Broadcasting Corporation, on air since 1981 with Inuktitut programming, and the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network, formed in 1999 with most programming by and for Aboriginal peoples, return control of the image, joined by Aboriginal-owned newspapers, radio, and production houses. Mainstream efforts count too: CBC's Beachcombers and North of 60 cast Aboriginal actors, Tina Keeper and Tom Jackson among them, as believable people with jobs, becoming for many viewers the only non-stereotype information they own. In print and galleries, Alberta artists like Dale Auger, Alex Janvier, Jane Ash Poitras, and Joane Cardinal-Schubert seized the pen back from centuries of European-perspective accounts.

Marketing and humour test who controls the symbol. The Braves' tomahawk chop, Chief Wahoo's grin, and the Edmonton Eskimos name sell stereotypes back to fans, and the Yankees or Fighting Irish defense fails because those groups never bore this legacy; tomahawks, feathers, and drums become toys emptied of spiritual weight. Humour cuts both ways: laughing at a target bonds the laughers through exclusion, and staying silent in that room is its own lesson. Don Burnstick of the Alexander First Nation reverses the current, telling redskin jokes, filet bologna and dozens more in the NFB's Redskins, Tricksters, and Puppy Stew, on the theory he states plainly: the word was racist, so he jumped into that racism, twisted it, and made it funny. Kainai actor Carl Brave Rock names the destination, young people longing not for the old big-nosed mean Indian but for a new stereotype, or better, none, while Inuit artist Kananginak Pootoogook's First Tourist freezes the hunter in a snapshot and asks who the exhibit really is.

example.title: Bank 3.1's stereotypes
example.text: Pair one screen stereotype (western bad guys, eco-guardians, mascot grins) with one breaker (APTN, North of 60, Burnstick's twist). That pair plus Lesson 1's headdress is more evidence than 3.1 needs, so pick your strongest two.

check.prompt: How can humour both build and break stereotypes?
check.sample: Sample response: laughing at a group bonds the laughers by excluding the target, but comedians like Burnstick seize the slur and twist it, draining its power by making the audience laugh with the target instead.
